reasoning: Everyday Palestinian formula said when worried about what may come, literally 'may God cover/protect'. The ت and س are plain, not emphatic.
Collective noun for fish. A single fish is samake.
ص is emphatic, so a capital S. Common everyday word for sidewalk or platform.
The Levantine pronunciation is leera, with ee. Taa marbuta after ر is a. Palestinians use the word for the lira of Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, while their own everyday currency is the shekel.
Palestinian bti- prefix with 3rif, then the subjunctive tsuu' with a glottal ق, as in everyday 'drive'. Some speakers say bta3rif, so the prefix vowel is the less certain part.

Core Palestinian political term in daily use. حق has a doubled glottal stop: 7a''. Taa marbuta after د is e. The aw diphthong is kept in this formal word, though some speakers may say 3oode. In formal speech ق may be [q].
Form X active participle with the colloquial mi- prefix and a medial glottal stop. The word is MSA-origin but used in real conversation about rentals. Some speakers say musta'jir.
أوضة is the usual Palestinian word for room, with emphatic ض. In the construct state the taa marbuta becomes t (ooDit); ooDet is also possible. The glottal is written inside the token after il-.
Literally 'end of the week', the normal Palestinian way to say weekend. The initial alif is a vowel seat, so nothing is written for it, but the glottal after il- is written.
Plural meaning baked savoury pastries (manaaqiish, sfiiHa and similar), the usual bakery term. Shadda on ج doubles it: 3ajjan. The prefix vowel may be mi- for some speakers.
Colloquial reassurance meaning God is great, so it will work out. The initial كْ cluster is Palestinian kbiir.
Imperfect yi3iin plus the object suffix -ni gives a doubled nn, though the script writes a single ن. Said when overwhelmed or facing a hard task.
Typical taxi or fare question frame. ق is a glottal stop and the shadda doubles d: bi'addeesh. The ellipsis is the blank for the destination and is not romanized.
ween is the Palestinian 'where' and il- is the article, left open for the noun to follow. The ellipsis and question mark are not romanized.
bi + il- gives bil-, and the glottal of aakhir is written inside the token. Respelled with ل to show bil-. A common everyday adverb.
Country name, also the city of Algiers. The medial hamza is a glottal stop. ج is a moon letter, so the article stays il-.
The demonstrative prefix ha + il- contracts to hal-. The glottal is written inside the token. Respelled with ل and sukun so the vowel is short.
ween is the Palestinian 'where'. Form VIII imperfect bti- + shtighil. The question mark is not romanized.
The meaning 'commented' points to form II 3alla' (3ala), e.g. commenting on a post, not 3ili' 'got stuck'. ق is read as a glottal stop as in the everyday 'hung'. Formal speakers may say [q].
The long vowel is ee: ba3deen. Very common everyday adverb meaning later or then.
Standard colloquial 'busy', with sh + gh and a long uu.
Form II with a doubled j. Besides 'encouraged', it is also the normal verb for cheering on or supporting a team.
Form I 7aDar means attended or was present. The English rules out form II 7aDDar 'prepared'. ح is 7 and ض is emphatic D.
Long o as in hoon, not u: looz. Collective noun for almonds.

French loanword. The spelling with ي suggests a long final vowel, and the unstressed first vowel usually drops. For the room itself, Palestinians usually say 7ammaam. The exact vowelling of the loan varies.
